title: Eclipsed Moon at Paranal
caption: Total lunar eclipse above the Very Large Telescope, Paranal Observatory, Chile
celestial: Photograph taken at Paranal Observatory, Chile

recognition.text: ESO Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: The eclipsed Moon hangs just above the domes of ESO's Very Large Telescope, as if the telescope were holding it up, like Atlas supporting the sky in Greek myth. The Moon glows faintly in the early morning twilight during a total lunar eclipse over Paranal Observatory in Chile's Atacama Desert.

The shot took careful planning. Astrophotographer Yuri Beletsky used precise calculations to find a spot nine kilometers east of Paranal, where the setting, eclipsed Moon would briefly line up just over the telescope domes.

A total lunar eclipse happens when the Earth passes directly between the Sun and the Moon. The Earth's shadow blocks direct sunlight, so the only light reaching the Moon has been bent through Earth's atmosphere, which gives it a reddish color. Because that light has been filtered by our atmosphere, astronomers use eclipses to study the signatures life leaves in an atmosphere, useful in the search for life on other planets.

understand.summary: This is a landscape photograph near ESO's Paranal Observatory, in visible light. The camera settings and color processing are not published.
understand.eye: The camera exposure brings out the faintly glowing eclipsed Moon more clearly than it might appear in the bright twilight to the eye.
